# Pedro F. Rackebrandt: research in full

> Every paper summary from https://rackebrandt.pe/, as plain text.

## When regimes cycle

Pedro F. Rackebrandt, 2026. Working paper. Topic: Regimes. Tags: Nonlinear dynamics, Political economy, V-Dem. Page: https://rackebrandt.pe/papers/when-regimes-cycle/

Many countries swing between democracy and autocracy for decades. Polybius called it anacyclosis. In my model the swings need no run of bad luck: the economy decides when they start and when they stop.

One quantity does the work: the pool of young people free to be mobilized. Below a threshold, a shock sets off swings that shrink each round. Above it, the swings never die out and the country keeps cycling. Falling behind your neighbours fills the pool and lifts a country over. A crisis erodes institutions and drops it back below.

Three predictions follow. Young autocracies that fall behind their neighbours open up. Crises keep autocracies shut and break young democracies. New autocracies often fall when a neighbour turns democratic, until they consolidate. All three hold in V-Dem data from 1950 to 2019, under eight different codings of regime type.

How to read the figure:

One flat axis runs from closed to open rule; the other is how mobilized people are. Height is the pool of young people, and the dashed square marks the threshold. The blue line is the country’s path and the red dot is where it stands now.

The arrows step through three stories. On the last slide you run the country yourself. Drag the figure to rotate it.

### The question

Many countries swing between democracy and autocracy for decades. Polybius called the pattern anacyclosis. Do the swings need a run of bad luck, or do they have an engine of their own? In this model they have one, and the economy decides when it starts and when it stops.

### The model

A country is two numbers, measured around its steady state: inclusiveness $x$, how open its institutions are, and mobilization $m$, how many of its people are mobilized. Mobilization has a ceiling $K$: the pool of young people free to be mobilized. Institutions absorb activists, and $h$ is the time they need per activist. The structure is the Rosenzweig and MacArthur model from population ecology.

> Inclusive institutions exist only if $v > c\eta$: an elite's gain from absorbing an opponent, $v$, must exceed the cost of keeping institutions open, $c\eta$. Otherwise $x \to 0$ from every starting point.

### The threshold

One number decides the dynamics:

$$K^* = \frac{1}{h} + 2m^*$$

where $m^*$ is mobilization at the steady state. Below $K^*$ the steady state is a stable focus: after a shock the country spirals back in loops. Above it the steady state loses stability and a limit cycle appears. This is a Hopf bifurcation.

Near the threshold the dynamics reduce to the Hopf normal form. Write $r$ for the distance from the steady state and $\varphi$ for the phase of the loop:

$$\dot r = \mu\, r - r^3, \qquad \dot\varphi = \omega, \qquad \mu \propto K - K^*$$

The loops take $2\pi/\omega$ to complete, the model's own period.

- If $K < K^*$, then $\mu < 0$ and $r \to 0$. Shocks fade in loops, so a new regime is safest at first and most at risk when the first swing comes back.
- If $K > K^*$, then $\mu > 0$ and $r \to \sqrt{\mu}$. The country keeps cycling, and the cycle starts small: its size grows with $\sqrt{K - K^*}$.

### What moves a country across

Falling behind the neighbours enlarges the pool of young people and raises $K$. A crisis speeds the erosion of institutions, which drops the country below the threshold and closes the regime. New autocracies also respond to an outside pull toward reopening, which acts only until they consolidate.

### The evidence

The tests use V-Dem from 1950 to 2019 and repeat under eight codings of regime type. All three predictions hold:

1. Young autocracies that fall behind their neighbours open up.
2. Crises keep autocracies shut and break young democracies.
3. New autocracies often fall when a neighbour turns democratic, until they consolidate.

### What it means

The cycle is conditional. The economy sets which side of $K^*$ a country sits on, and one pool of young people answers two triggers: relative decline opens autocracies, outright crisis breaks young democracies. The thresholds also say what any shock must move to matter: $v$ against $c\eta$, or $h$ and with it $K^*$.

## How many tests was it really?

Pedro F. Rackebrandt, Sebastian Winzker, 2026. Working paper. Topic: Finance. Tags: Deflated Sharpe, Quantitative Finance. Page: https://rackebrandt.pe/papers/how-many-tests/

Why does this matter? When you test thousands of trading rules, the best one will look good by chance. Cluster corrections that group similar rules can make noise look significant by undercounting the tests. A block bootstrap on the real grid keeps the correlations and shows the safer hurdle is the full nominal count.

We resample the 2,825 moving-average rules together. On the DAX the effective independent tests are about 1,400. Even spread-out correlation barely lowers that number; only rules bunched in blocks do. The best rule still fails the hurdle on the DAX.

How to read the figure:

The curve is the expected maximum Sharpe ratio if every rule is noise. It grows like the square root of log N, so only the order of magnitude of N matters. The buttons read the hurdle at the cluster, effective, and nominal counts.

Software that clusters similar moving averages reports N = 2. That point sits far below the measured hurdle. The measured effective count is about 1,400. Using the raw grid of 2,825 overstates the hurdle by 6 percent.

On the DAX the best rule clears the mean of the noise maximum and still fails the 95 percent band.

### The question

Every parameter search is a multiple test. The best of many noisy rules looks good by chance, so the bar it must clear rises with the number of rules tried. A grid of moving average rules holds thousands of settings, and neighbouring settings trade almost alike. How many independent tests does such a grid represent, and what does that count do to the bar?

### The hurdle

Bailey and López de Prado (2014) give the Sharpe ratio that the best of $N$ independent noise strategies reaches on average:

$$\begin{aligned} \widehat{SR}_0 = \mathrm{E}\Big[\max_n \widehat{SR}_n\Big] \approx \sigma_{SR}\Big[&(1-\gamma)\,\Phi^{-1}\Big(1-\frac{1}{N}\Big) \\ &+\gamma\,\Phi^{-1}\Big(1-\frac{1}{N e}\Big)\Big] \end{aligned}$$

Here $\widehat{SR}_n$ is the estimated Sharpe ratio of trial $n$, $\sigma_{SR}$ the spread of those estimates across trials, $\Phi^{-1}$ the inverse of the standard normal distribution function, $\gamma \approx 0.5772$ the Euler Mascheroni constant and $e$ Euler's number. The hurdle grows like $\sqrt{\ln N}$, so only the order of magnitude of $N$ matters.

The deflated Sharpe ratio is the probability that the chosen rule's true Sharpe ratio beats that hurdle:

$$\mathrm{DSR} = \Phi\!\left(\frac{\big(\widehat{SR}-\widehat{SR}_0\big)\sqrt{T-1}}{\sqrt{1-\hat{S}\,\widehat{SR}+\dfrac{\hat{K}-1}{4}\,\widehat{SR}^{2}}}\right)$$

$\widehat{SR}$ is the chosen rule's Sharpe ratio, $T$ the number of returns, $\hat{S}$ their skewness and $\hat{K}$ their kurtosis (3 for normal returns). The denominator is the estimation error of a Sharpe ratio; fat tails and negative skew widen it.

### Counting the tests

We run a stationary block bootstrap on the full grid of 2,825 moving average rules. Each replicate draws the same trading days for every rule, in blocks of random length with mean ten days, so the correlation between rules survives. The best Sharpe ratio in each replicate gives the null distribution of the maximum. The effective number of tests $N_{\text{eff}}$ is the count that makes the formula return the bootstrap's expected maximum:

$$\begin{aligned} \mathrm{E}^{*}\Big[\max_n \widehat{SR}_n\Big] = \sigma_{SR}\Big[&(1-\gamma)\,\Phi^{-1}\Big(1-\frac{1}{N_{\text{eff}}}\Big) \\ &+\gamma\,\Phi^{-1}\Big(1-\frac{1}{N_{\text{eff}}\,e}\Big)\Big] \end{aligned}$$

$\mathrm{E}^{*}$ is the average over bootstrap replicates. The right side rises with $N_{\text{eff}}$, so one value solves it.

### The result

On the DAX, $N_{\text{eff}}$ is about 1,400. Software that clusters similar moving averages reports $N = 2$. Cluster corrections of this kind cut the hurdle by as much as 84 percent and call noise significant. The raw count of 2,825 overstates it by 6 percent.

Why so little shrinkage? A correlation shared evenly by all rules moves the whole grid up and down together. It shrinks the expected maximum and the spread $\sigma_{SR}$ by the same factor, so the formula still needs the full $N$. Only block structure lowers $N_{\text{eff}}$: rules inside a tight block act as one. Of the eigenvalue corrections, only Gao (2008) stays close.

What moves the required Sharpe ratio:

| Source | Effect |
|---|---|
| Multiplicity | factor of 7.3 |
| $N_{\text{eff}}$ in place of $N$ | minus 3.1 percent |
| Daily non normality | plus 0.2 percent |

The best moving average rule survives in 3 of 17 markets and 2 of 31 German stocks. On the DAX it clears the mean of the noise maximum and fails the 95 percent band.

### What it means

The hurdle grows so slowly in $N$ that counting too many trials costs little, while counting too few costs a lot. The block bootstrap on the real grid shows the nominal count is the safe one.

## Reversed by our own replication

Pedro F. Rackebrandt, 2026. Working paper. Topic: AI. Tags: Verification, Multi-model. Page: https://rackebrandt.pe/papers/reversed-by-replication/

Why does this matter? An automated auditor that checks research extractions is right only about a third of the time, yet a wrong extraction can still return a theorem. We pre-registered three signals that might catch the error, then tested them once on frontier models. Two reversed. Cross-model disagreement is the one that held.

On 174 items, a model disagreeing with its own repeats cleared the bar in only one family. Disagreement across models reached 0.75 and stayed above the threshold. It flagged errors better on unconventional designs. Abstaining where models disagree most trims the error rate from 81% to 72%, but the tool remains weak.

How to read the figure:

Each row is a registered comparison. The open square is the discovery sample on five open-weight arms. The filled circle is the confirmatory run on four frontier families. The dashed navy line is the 0.65 threshold we deposited before seeing those families. The dotted line is chance.

Task structure falls from 0.771 to about 0.50 and is retracted. Within-model sampling falls from 0.727 and clears the bar in one family of four. Cross-model disagreement rises from 0.609 to 0.753 and is held.

### The question

A causal claim rests on its identification: treatment, outcome, controls, design. Given that specification, identification algorithms (Shpitser and Pearl; Jaber et al.) decide whether the effect can be recovered. The weak step is reading the paper into the specification. Language models now do that reading, most of their extractions fail the benchmark's grader, and a wrong specification still returns a verdict.

Does disagreement among extractions flag the wrong ones, item by item and with no answer key, well enough to tell a pipeline when to abstain?

### The design

The corpus is CausalReasoningBenchmark (Sawarni, Tan, Syrgkanis): 174 items, each with an expert specification. The authors' grader, `evaluate_identification`, scores each model's modal answer, the specification it returns most often across its draws. The error $e^f_i$ is 1 if the grader rejects family $f$'s modal answer on item $i$, and 0 otherwise.

Five open weight arms served as the discovery sample and named three candidate signals. The decision rules were then registered on OSF on 13 September 2026, with the hash of the analysis script deposited, and run once on four frontier families: Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and xAI, three draws each at temperature 1.0. That is 2,088 extractions.

### The signals

- **Within model disagreement** $d^{W,f}_i$: how far family $f$'s three draws on item $i$ differ.
- **Cross model disagreement** $d^{C}_i$: how far the four families differ on item $i$.
- **Task structure** $k^f_i$: the number of design fields in family $f$'s predicted specification.

Each signal $s$ is judged by its AUROC, written $A(s)$: the probability that a randomly drawn wrong item scores higher than a randomly drawn right one.

$$A(s) = \Pr\big(s_i > s_j \mid e_i = 1,\ e_j = 0\big)$$

Ties count as half. Chance is 0.5; perfect separation is 1. With $f$ running over the four families, the registered rules were:

$$\begin{aligned} \text{C1:}&\quad \#\{f : A(d^{W,f}) \ge 0.65\} \ge 3 \\ \text{C2:}&\quad A(d^{C}) \ge 0.65 \\ \text{C3:}&\quad \#\{f : A(k^{f}) > A(d^{W,f})\} \ge 3 \end{aligned}$$

### The result

| Rule | Discovery | Frontier | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| C1 Within model | 0.727 | 0.680, Google only | Failed |
| C2 Cross model | 0.609 | 0.753, interval [0.661, 0.840] | Held |
| C3 Task structure | 0.771 | about 0.50, one family | Retracted |

A registered falsifier predicted that families would agree on the same wrong answer for unconventional designs. Disagreement separated errors better there: 0.868 against 0.646, permutation $p = 0.025$. Neither ensemble breadth nor model accuracy explains the reversal.

Abstaining where the families disagree most lowers the error on what is kept:

$$\bar e_{\text{all}} = 80.9\% \;\longrightarrow\; \bar e_{H} = 72.4\%$$

$H$ is the half of the items with the lowest $d^{C}_i$, and $\bar e$ is the share of graded answers that are wrong.

### What it means

The signal ranked last in discovery is the only one that survived. Five open weight arms favoured task structure and within model sampling; four frontier families reversed both. Cross model disagreement worked best on unconventional designs, the case the falsifier expected to break it. As an abstention rule it cuts error by 8.5 points, and the half it keeps is still wrong 72.4 percent of the time.
